arrival.note: A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. tax_1833 stands against this person's name by 31 December 1833 and nothing says when they came. THE 1833 TAX LIST IS A PROPERTY ROLL, NOT A RESIDENCE CHECK (T-1117): it names the owner of ground inside the town, resident or not, and its own entry 110 is a man three years dead. It bounds the town's RECORD of this name and not the day this person reached Chicago. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the town's own paper carries this name by 1 July 1835; whether the man it names was standing in the town is a claim this record cannot make, and present_on_scene_date says `uncertain` for that reason.

It says what a household of this bound most likely was, and nothing whatever about this household.

present_on_scene_date.note: THE RECORD DOES NOT REACH THE DAY. Every source that names this person falls on one side of 1 July 1835, and nothing follows them to it or says they left. `uncertain` rather than dropped — the distinction index.json draws for Jeremiah Porter, and a finding, not a gap. AND THE BRACKET THIS CARD ONCE HAD IS WITHDRAWN, NOT LOST: its at-or-before leg was tax_1833 alone. THE 1833 TAX LIST IS A PROPERTY ROLL, NOT A RESIDENCE CHECK (T-1117): it names the owner of ground inside the town, resident or not, and its own entry 110 is a man three years dead. It bounds the town's RECORD of this name and not the day this person reached Chicago, so it cannot say this person was here to be followed across the day. Withdrawn to `uncertain` and not to `absent` — no source places this person anywhere else on 1 July 1835 either, and a man who was taxed for ground in the town may perfectly well have been standing on it.

dated_bounds.note: PROPERTY, NOT PRESENCE (T-1117). Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 names the owners of ground inside the town, resident or not — its entry 110 is Alexander Wolcott, who had been dead since 25 October 1830 — so this row bounds what this person was assessed for and says nothing about where the person was. tools/assert_tax_roll_ruling.py holds that ruling on the two readings it rests on. THE IDENTITY IS INFERRED AND THE PAGE IS NOT. The reading of the roll is documented — the town's own paper, held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository, twice mediated by Schulz's transcription and Genealogy Trails' republication, which this project has not gone behind. What no source states is that the man on the roll is the person on this card: data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json joins them on a name, by its rule “one resident of the surname 'Jones' agrees with the entry's forenames; 6 bearer(s) of the surname were considered.”, and forenames agree initial for initial: entry 'D. E. Jones' against resident 'D E Jones'. A bound whose subject is inferred is an inferred bound. No grade moves here and the identity is neither reopened nor hardened.

Read from tax_1833. THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G3), applied to every identity at once by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py and spent onto this card by tools/mint_civic_residents.py; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. tax_1833 stands against this person's name by 31 December 1833 and nothing says when they came. THE 1833 TAX LIST IS A PROPERTY ROLL, NOT A RESIDENCE CHECK (T-1117): it names the owner of ground inside the town, resident or not, and its own entry 110 is a man three years dead. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the town's own paper carries this name by 1 July 1835; whether the man it names was standing in the town is a claim this record cannot make, and present_on_scene_date says `uncertain` for that reason. No figure is drawn (L1). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Jones, D. E.” (tax_1833_052, line 104). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Jones' agrees with the entry's forenames; 5 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

age_band.note: AN AGE BAND, NEVER A YEAR. No source this project holds bears on when this person was born, so the band is drawn from the only committed sex by age distribution the project has - the 1840 Chicago schedule, five years after the scene and a town twice the size - seeded by this person's own id ('jones_d_e:age_bands_1840'). AND THE CONDITIONING IS THE MODEL'S, NOT A SOURCE'S: that a poll, tax or muster list names a person 20 or over - the 1840 schedule's own adult line. THE FRANCHISE'S AGE RULE IS NOT IN ANY SOURCE RECORD THIS PROJECT HOLDS; this is the model's conditioning and not a reading (T-1303's finding, handed to T-1304). No exact year is written, because a year drawn from a decadal band would read as a record of a birth.

old_settler_deaths.the_header_admission:
Names, places * , dates, and ages at death
of some of Chicago's Old Settlers, prior to 1843, and other well - known citizens who arrived after 1843, together
with others prominently connected with Illinois history:
old_settler_deaths.note: LATER EVIDENCE OF A DEATH, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. Fergus's 1843 directory (1896) prints an obituary list of old settlers, and one of its entries meets somebody of this name. THE HEADER OF THE LIST IS QUOTED ABOVE, and it is the limit the whole reading turns on. It does not mean the person was in Chicago in 1835, and it does not mean they arrived before 1843 — the list's own header, quoted above, says it also names citizens who arrived later and others merely 'prominently connected with Illinois history'. A match means one thing: a name in the 1835 layer and a name in this list agree on surname and first initial, and the list gives that name a death date and an age. The date and the interval are the payload. Whatever is carried is carried as evidence of a DEATH and of an interval the birth falls in, never as an 1835 fact and never as a grade. T-0513 consolidates and T-0514/T-0515 apply; this file changes no record. THE AGREEMENT HERE IS A SURNAME AND ONE INITIAL: one of the two sides prints an initial where the forename would be, so a single letter is the whole of the discriminator and the match is as thin as the rule allows. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. A death notice printed in 1896 says a person of this name died on a day; under the ratified ladder (T-0513) that is later evidence about a DEATH, and it is never an 1835 residence. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

people.matched_by: Surname 'Jones' folds to the same string as the entry's, and the given name of both begins D.
people.birth_year_arithmetic: The page prints the death as 'January 11, 1886' and the age as 'aged 78'. An age of 78 completed years means at least 78 and less than 79, so the birth falls between 1807-01-12 and 1808-01-11: the birth year is 1807 or 1808. The subtraction is this project's; the page states no year of birth.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. WHAT THIS PASS RULED ONTO THIS HOUSEHOLD, named so the ruling can be found again: each volume below is followed by the printed entries it set against this person and the status the crosswalk ruled them at — a single entry carries what its own `could_carry` declares, and an ambiguous or contested match carries nothing and is shown so that the silence is legible. jones_d_e, Fergus's Chicago directory of 1843 — f1843_e1423, f1843_e1424, f1843_e1425 (ambiguous, so nothing crossed); jones_d_e, the advertising cards in Norris's directory of 1844 — n1844_ad0036 (a single entry).

occupation_later.note: The advertising cards in Norris's directory of 1844 prints this trade against this person, in the entry quoted on the card: 'D. A. Jones'. It is evidence about 1844, written here as 1844's and read back onto no 1835 claim. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. The value is the volume's own line, split by its crosswalk on the entry's punctuation. These volumes set the trade first and its qualifiers after it on the same line, so the split may carry an employer, a market or a corner along with the trade. The printed entry is quoted beside the value for exactly that reason: the split is checkable against it, and neither is read into an 1835 claim.
